questions.q: Define "contextual meaning" of a word in poetry and explain how it differs from dictionary meaning, using one example from "ckny jkx".
questions.a: Contextual meaning is the specific sense a word acquires from its syntactic position, imagery, and thematic role within the poem — e.g., "ckny" in the poem does not merely mean "absence of light" (dictionary) but signifies colonial oppression, ignorance, and spiritual stagnation. A wrong answer that only gives the dictionary definition reveals the student treats poetic language as transparent labeling rather than condensed signification.

questions.q: The NCERT glosses "foIyo" as "Økafr] ck<+". In stanza 2, the line reads "foIyo&jo ls NksVs gh gSa 'kksHkk ikrs". Explain why the poet chooses "foIyo" instead of simpler synonyms like "ckny" or "Andhera", and what the compound "foIyo&jo" adds to the image.
questions.a: "foIyo" (tatsama, from vi + ava + ya — "gone down, set") carries the connotation of a natural, cyclical sunset, unlike "ckny" which suggests unnatural, imposed darkness. "foIyo&jo" (twilight's yoke/pair) personifies dusk as a burdened laborer, foreshadowing the exploited masses in later stanzas. A wrong answer that treats "foIyo" as mere synonym for "evening" misses the poem's historical allegory: colonial rule as an unnatural "long night" masquerading as natural order.

questions.q: Analyze the morphological structure and contextual force of the compound "v'kfu&ikr" (stanza 3). Break it into components, identify the sandhi/samasa type, and explain how its meaning "otzikr" (terror-striking) transforms the description of the night.
questions.a: "v'kfu" (fear/terror) + "ikr" (doer/maker, from √kri) = bahuvrihi compound: "that which makes [others] fearful." The compound condenses a whole clause ("jo bhay paida kare") into a single epithet. Calling the night "v'kfu&ikr" shifts agency: darkness is not passive absence but an active agent of terror — mirroring how colonial power actively manufactures fear. A student who only writes "bhayankar" without analyzing the compound structure misses how Nirala's Sanskritized lexicon encodes resistance through grammatical density.

questions.q: Compare the words "jQ¼" (stanza 1) and "jksx" (stanza 4). Both relate to sound/voice. Using their glosses and stanza contexts, analyze how their connotations differ and what this contrast reveals about the poem's movement from despair to resistance.
questions.a: "jQ¼" (gloss: "jQdk gqvk" — broken, fractured) describes the night's silence as a shattered, helpless sound — the muted cry of the oppressed. "jksx" (in "jksx&'kksd") appears in "jksx&'kksd esa Hkh g¡lrk gS 'kS'ko dk lqoqQekj 'kjhj" — here, sound becomes "kS'ko" (uproar/revolt) with "lqoqQekj" (resounding). The shift from fractured whisper to collective roar maps the poem's trajectory: from individualized suffering to mass awakening. A wrong answer that treats both as "sound words" without tracking the semantic arc fails to see vocabulary as narrative engine.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The NCERT glossary (jQ¼) entries for this poem are sufficient for board exam vocabulary questions." Defend or critique with specific examples from the poem.
questions.a: Critique: The glossary covers only 15 selected words, mostly tatsama compounds. It omits key tadbhava/descriptive words like "fiQj&fiQj" (repeated flickering), "pwl" (moment), "gkM+&ek=k" (deep stake/claim) whose contextual meanings are essential for "explain with reference to context" questions. For instance, "gkM+&ek=k" glossed as "vkèkkj" (rooted) in the glossary, but in "gkM+&ek=k gh gS vkèkkj" it means "inalienable right/claim" — a legal-political term crucial for the poem's rights-discourse. A student relying solely on the glossary will miss the vocabulary of resistance embedded in everyday Hindi. This error reveals confusion between "glossary completion" and "vocabulary mastery."

Sample stanza:
